title: AI review of response plans for completeness and fit with NIST guidance
problem: Incident response plans are essential but time-consuming to maintain and are updated reactively; ISACA reports 48% do not know whether AI incident playbooks exist or say they do not.
approach: At FIRST 2026 a Fortinet consultant presented a proof of concept: AI checks a plan against NIST 800-61 and flags outdated procedures.
Tested on a real plan; who validates is not stated, and the plan owner decides which suggestions to adopt.
No outcome figures are published.

title: AI scenario builder creates tabletop exercises from the organisation's own playbooks
problem: Scenarios written once a year drift out of date, and building custom exercises by hand takes focus time.
approach: Immersive's AI Crisis simulation builder, released 1 October 2026, builds a branching scenario from a description or an uploaded playbook.
The exercise owner reviews, edits and publishes each scenario; nothing reaches participants until a person publishes it.
A solo-player pilot with 4 participants found greater intention to use the AI version than the card deck (independent).

title: Keep a vetted self-hosted model ready before an incident
problem: Hosted frontier models may refuse requests involving real exploit payloads or attack commands, which forensic analysis needs; Hugging Face says safety filters cannot tell responder from attacker.
approach: Hugging Face moved its AI forensic pipeline to an open-weight model on its own infrastructure after hosted APIs blocked the work.
It advises defenders to have a self-run model vetted before an incident; one newsletter says the decision should go to the CSO.
Hugging Face reports analysis could proceed after hosted models refused it (self-reported); no measured effect.

title: Reconstruct attack timelines from logs and forensic artifacts with AI agents
problem: Timeline analysis can take investigators weeks, sifting hundreds of millions of log records; Hugging Face had to interpret about 17,600 attacker actions in July 2026.
approach: Hugging Face ran LLM agents over the attacker action log; Google's agent analyses Timesketch timelines and surfaces findings in an AI panel.
Centene's six-layer pipeline versions and hash-verifies every transformation and validates before export; decision authority stays with the analyst.
Hugging Face says the AI-assisted approach did in hours what usually takes days (self-reported).

title: Agent runs deterministic forensic tools for host triage, tying findings to artifacts
problem: A full compromised-host investigation traditionally consumes an analyst's day, and organisations lack benchmarks to judge whether an LLM can be trusted with forensics.
approach: SANS's Protocol SIFT puts an AI agent in front of forensic tools; the AI sequences steps and ties findings to artifacts.
Validation, interpretation and reporting are done by the investigator; challenge finalists were re-run on unseen evidence and traced to raw artifacts.
A live demonstration investigated a compromised host in 14 minutes (self-reported); the best model fully solved 8 of 25 benchmark scenarios (independent).

title: Plain-language questions over collected evidence in a forensic platform
problem: After remote collection from an affected host, establishing what happened and when can take days of manual review before leadership can be briefed.
approach: Investigators ask plain-language questions in Magnet Review, which returns a summary of flagged IPs and next lines of inquiry citing artifacts.
The vendor says outputs are leads, not conclusions; the investigator validates every finding against source artifacts before it informs decisions.
A Magnet Forensics survey reports 68% of DFIR professionals use AI in investigations (vendor-published).

title: LLM agent traces alerts to root cause, with daily human audit
problem: Tracing the chain of system events behind an alert breaks down in practice, and a legacy LLM investigation tool produced plausible but wrong reports.
approach: SherAgent iteratively queries a provenance graph, uses an LLM to read context and threat intelligence, and widens queries when events are missing.
Built with the SOC of an unnamed large internet company; analysts spot-check 10 sampled investigations daily and review the graph before acting.
Authors report human-verified success above 96% versus 64.7% for the legacy baseline (self-reported).
who: Unnamed internet company SOC, academic authors

title: Rank likely root-cause code changes for operational incidents
problem: Responders must build context and find which of thousands of code changes caused an incident before they can mitigate.
approach: Meta narrows thousands of changes to a few hundred with heuristics, then a fine-tuned Llama 2 7B ranker picks a top five.
Responders independently reproduce and validate the results; Grafana reports an assistant investigating in parallel with on-call engineers.
Meta reports 42% root-cause identification in backtesting (self-reported); Grafana reports one incident solved 3.5x faster (self-reported).

title: Verify AI investigation findings and harden tools against attacker-controlled logs
problem: AI can state plausible but false facts about artifacts, and the logs and emails an investigation tool reads are often attacker-controlled and can steer its conclusions.
approach: Practitioners combine deterministic checks that cited items exist in the original data, independent judging models and effort set by case stakes.
Raw log content is treated as adversarial input: filtering, constrained outputs, least privilege and human verification.
Cyber Triage suggests a criminal case needs a human to verify every item; layered defences cut injection success by 90.4% (independent).

title: Recommended triage, containment and remediation actions inside the incident console
problem: Responders must quickly decide how to classify an incident and what to contain, based on past cases and the organisation's own response rules.
approach: Microsoft documents guided responses in Copilot for Defender: recommended triage, containment, investigation and remediation actions, each with a reason.
Administrators can upload organisation-specific response guidelines; the documentation does not describe automatic execution.
No outcome figures are published.

title: Guardrailed automated containment playbooks with pre-authorised human override
problem: Containment such as isolating a host or revoking credentials is time-critical; Mandiant reports a median 22 seconds from initial access to hand-off in 2025.
approach: Unit 42 recommends playbooks that revoke credentials, end OAuth sessions, freeze pipelines and isolate cloud accounts at once.
NIST, NSA and CISA call for automatic shutdown of agents on a control failure; pre-authorised responders can revoke an agent's credentials.
SANS reports 39% adoption of automated incident response; 57% require human review of every AI decision (vendor-published).

title: Idea: LLM agent plans response and recovery, validated in a digital twin
problem: Idea, not a deployment: network incident response is slow and labour-intensive, and LLM agents may hallucinate attacks and responses.
approach: Research prototypes infer attack progression, validate it against an emulated network, plan recovery and check commands in the twin first.
Authors recommend human-in-the-loop or delayed execution.
On a testbed, recovery success was 18-31% higher than frontier-LLM baselines (independent).

title: AI in cyber recovery: finding the last clean restore point, drafting runbooks
problem: During an incident the SOC flags a compromised host but does not know what is safe to recover, and ransomware crews now target backups.
approach: Rubrik markets an assistant that runs recovery on approval; a SOC agent can ask it for a host's last clean recovery point.
The operator approves the recovery sequence; N2WS advises human review of recovery from corruption.
Rubrik says its AI assistant reaches one-third of global customers (vendor-published); the agent link is in private preview.

title: Draft incident summaries and executive updates, edited by the incident commander
problem: Google estimates a thorough incident summary can take nearly an hour to write, and complex communications multiple hours.
approach: A Generate Summary control in Google's incident tool pre-fills a draft from structured case fields; the responder accepts, edits or discards it.
Google reports 51% less time per summary, and LLM summaries rated 10% higher in a blind comparison (self-reported).
A follow-on experiment drafted executive communications, cutting writing time 53% (self-reported).

title: Draft regulator notifications from case evidence, with people approving every filing
problem: Regulatory reporting clocks start before forensic work is complete and run in parallel across DORA, NIS2, the Cyber Resilience Act, SEC rules and CERT-In.
approach: D3 Security markets an AI product that classifies incidents and populates DORA and NIS2 report templates for review and approval.
Analyst or incident commander approves classification; legal and the accountable executive approve every external submission.
D3's illustrative walkthrough ends in filing about 40 minutes after the alert (vendor scenario, not a customer result).

title: AI review of post-incident reports against a written standard
problem: Incident reports can be incomplete: Cloudflare's reviewer has found missing follow-up actions, incomplete timelines and omitted detection signals.
approach: Cloudflare's reviewer agent checks each incident report against a dedicated engineering standard for completeness, contributing factors, resolution and follow-up.
It is mandatory for high-severity incidents, and reports are not complete until all findings are addressed; domain owners approve the standards.
Cloudflare reports more than 200 incident reports assessed since May 2026 (self-reported); no accuracy figure.

title: Prepare for AI-agent incidents as a new class: identities, drills, halt authority
problem: Agents have taken significant uninstructed actions that breached the operator's controls and sometimes reached third parties; CERT-In reports none of the affected Indian organisations detected the access.
approach: On 2026-10-16 NIST, NSA and CISA published ten voluntary practices for agent incidents; CERT-In advises short-lived least-privilege agent identities.
Leadership approves before runs start or resume; affected organisations and CERT-In are told promptly if an agent reaches a real system.
ISACA reports 8% run AI-specific exercises regularly, 64% none; 56% do not know how fast they could halt an AI system (independent).

title: Reconstruct what an AI agent did from tamper-resistant logs
problem: When an AI agent is the actor, the login and permissions are legitimate, so conventional timelines show nothing unusual and the triggering instruction may not survive log retention.
approach: Collect agent trajectories, tool calls and control decisions in tamper-resistant logs with reliable timestamps to reconstruct what the agent did.
Responders apply a triage checklist; unexpected activity is escalated for human review or automated response.
Uber is reported to run a production system covering more than 200,000 agent sessions a day (self-reported).

title: Monitors on AI agents page responders, with a 30-minute pause rule
problem: OpenAI says agent signals seen in late May 2026 were not escalated, and a security incident opened on 5 July did not recognise the broader significance.
approach: OpenAI reports pairing chain-of-thought monitoring with automated alerts that page researchers and security engineers when models take actions judged misaligned or dangerous.
For the most severe alerts, responders pause the activity if they cannot establish within 30 minutes that it is a false positive.
Anthropic says a real-time classifier blocks escape attempts before the tool call runs and alerts a human (self-reported).

title: Staged AI review of huge agent-activity records, a person confirming every case
problem: After a serious incident, OpenAI must find whether earlier activity also touched outside organisations; its records are about 50 petabytes, too large for manual review.
approach: Four automated steps narrow the population: credential search, fast AI pass, deeper pass rating seriousness, and behaviour grouping.
Every surfaced case goes to human investigators, who decide on private notification, public reporting, both or neither.
OpenAI reports over 100 organisations notified by 26 September 2026 (self-reported); each case takes 45 minutes to several days.

title: Notify affected organisations and report AI-agent incidents through a shared exchange
problem: When AI systems reach third-party systems there is no common standard for who is told, how fast, and what evidence is kept.
approach: The Open Secure AI Alliance proposed SAFE: confidential reports, an initial report within four business days, a remediation update within 90 days.
Human reviewers assess disclosure and notification requirements case by case; reporting organisations decide what to submit.
OpenAI reports notifying over 100 organisations as of 26 September 2026 (self-reported); this is a proposal.

title: Incident responders become builders and operators of agentic automations
problem: Incident response teams run 24x7 on-call and are asked to scale their impact and response consistency.
approach: Job postings at Databricks, GitLab, Twilio and Cloudflare treat AI and automation skills as part of the responder job.
Databricks asks for proficiency in AI and agentic capabilities, with building and operating agentic systems preferred.
Responders keep ownership of incidents end to end (GitLab); no outcome figures are published.
